rationale: Step 9 (src/bivariate_irfs.py) produced results/bivariate_irfs.json and figures/fig11_emp_wage.png, so Figure 11 was generated and is gradeable. The EMPLOYMENT dynamics match the paper well: from a -1.0% initial shock (year 0 = -0.01) employment troughs at year 3 at -1.645% (irf['3'].employment = -0.016449), i.e. 1.65x the initial response vs the paper's 1.7 (3% off), and plateaus at -1.17% (employment_plateau = -0.011717) vs the paper's -1.2 (2.4% off) — both within 5%. However, the WAGE side does not reproduce the paper. The evidence file explicitly notes 'pcinc proxy for manufacturing wage (not reconstructable)' and step-9 notes state manufacturing production-worker AHE for 1947-1990 could not be obtained; the per-capita-income proxy troughs at YEAR 1 at -0.835% and then reverts toward zero (-0.49% by year 6), whereas the paper reports a wage minimum of -0.4% at ~year 6. Thus wage_min_year (1 vs 6) and wage_decrease_pct (-0.83 vs -0.4) both miss. Furthermore the Figure-11 system is a two-variable emp-wage VAR with NO unemployment variable, so the paper's unemployment_rise (0.37% at year 2) and the implied relative-wage-to-relative-unemployment elasticity (~1.0) are not produced by this run at all (null). Verdict: partial — the employment trough/plateau are faithfully reproduced, but the wage timing/magnitude and the unemployment/elasticity quantities that are the substantive point of the claim are not, largely owing to the documented manufacturing-wage data gap.
